notes_list.title: E/Z Nomenclature & CIP Priority Rules
notes_list.basic_overview: Geometrical isomerism arises due to restricted rotation around the C=C double bond. When all 4 groups attached to sp2 carbons are different, cis/trans nomenclature fails, and we use E/Z nomenclature based on Cahn-Ingold-Prelog (CIP) priority rules.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Z = Zusammen (German for 'together' -> higher priority groups on the same side). E = Entgegen (German for 'opposite' -> higher priority groups on opposite sides, remember 'E' for Enemy/Opposite).
notes_list.examples: 1. 2-butene (CH3/H vs CH3/H). 2. Halogen-substituted alkenes (Br vs Cl vs F). 3. Isotopic substitution (D vs H). 4. Functional group comparison (-COOH vs -CH3).
notes_list.conditions_and_medium: Configurational isomers; interconversion requires breaking the π bond. Stereospecific reactions (like syn-addition) preserve or predictably alter this geometry.
notes_list.mechanism_steps: 1. Split C=C into left and right sp2 carbons. 2. Apply CIP Rule 1: Higher atomic number gets Priority 1. 3. Apply CIP Rule 2 (if atomic number ties): Compare atomic mass (isotopes like D > H) or move down the chain to the next atoms. 4. Apply CIP Rule 3 (multiple bonds): Treat double/triple bonds as bonded to 2/3 single atoms. 5. Compare spatial sides: Same side = Z, Opposite sides = E.
notes_list.kinetics_and_energy: High activation energy barrier prevents spontaneous room-temperature rotation around the C=C bond.
notes_list.selectivity_and_stereochemistry: Fundamental for predicting major stereoisomers in elimination (E2) and addition reactions.
notes_list.common_traps: Never judge priority by the physical size or length of a carbon chain; always evaluate atom-by-atom based on atomic number starting directly from the double-bonded carbon.

exam_focus.level: IIT-JAM / MSc entrance / GATE concept depth
